m01.B1_quote: I read the 114 grey values of the JPEG and printed them as a 19 × 6 grid.
m01.B2_quote: A wide band at this scale is consistent with a daily cycle squeezed into each column, but I can't confirm one.
m01.B4_quote: In columns 14–15 (roughly days 42–48) the top two rows are near-black. That is a burst of much higher values
m01.B6_quantity: I don't have a confident view, and nothing in the file can settle it. ... fits things like river level after a storm, air pollution during an episode, or wind speed during a gale. I would not choose between these
m01.B8_quote: Each pixel is enlarged into a 52 px cell ... Every hour is drawn as a dot at a fixed-seed random spot inside its cell.

m02.B1_quote: I found 1,439 dot centres. Where dots had merged into one blob, I split them by size.
m02.B2_quote: Checking how the series repeats over time showed its strongest period is 12.42 hours, not 24.
m02.B4_quote: one event near day 45. ... It peaks at about 188 px above the tidal prediction
m02.B5_quote: A smaller rise of the same kind shows around days 53–54.
m02.B6_quantity: hourly water level at a coastal tide gauge, over two months
m02.B8_quote: Each line is drawn through the actual hourly values, with one small dot per hour, like the original. The 25 filled-in hours are shown as open dots.

m03.B1_quote: I dumped all 1,725 grey values of `record.jpg` (75 × 23) as numbers and looked at them.
m03.B2_quote: That fits a quantity that swings within each day around a level that drifts slowly.
m03.B3_quote: The spacing is about 14 days, with strong and weak wide phases taking turns. That matches the spring–neap cycle of tides
m03.B4_quote: Around days 42–45 a single spike rises to roughly four times the band's usual height above its centre.
m03.B6_quantity: most likely a water level from a tide gauge on a sea with small tides, and that the spike is a storm surge
m03.B7_quote: Air pollution would be a plausible alternative, for example a fireworks spike. That would fit if the record spans New Year, but the file contains no dates to check.
m03.B8_quote: It enlarges the 75 × 23 grains as a faint grid, then puts back exactly 1,464 dots, one per hour, each assigned to the column it fell into and stacked vertically in proportion to the ink that column kept

m04.B1_quote: I opened it and printed all 75 × 23 grey values as ASCII ... I then saved the exact grey values and worked out, for each column, its weighted centre
m04.B2_quote: Its thickness suggests a lot of hour-to-hour change, perhaps a daily cycle, but the image can't confirm that.
m04.B4_quote: a single sharp rise at columns 53–55 (about days 42–45) climbs to the very top of the image
m04.B6_quantity: I can only describe the shape of the record, not name the quantity.
m04.B8_quote: the 75 × 23 pixels are enlarged exactly as they are, compression smudges included, into a large grid of grey cells.

m05.B1_quote: I read all 114 pixels as grey values. ... Working files (the pixel dump and screenshots)
m05.B2_quote: A daily cycle, which would separate temperature from these, is far too fine to survive 77-hour pixels.
m05.B4_quote: There is one short excursion to the very top, around days 41–48 (columns 13–14).
m05.B6_quantity: I can't say, and any guess would be weak.
m05.B8_quote: Which of the six bands an hour lands in is decided by lot, weighted by how grey its pixel is. ... the line runs the full height of the band

m06.B1_quote: I printed the grey value of every one of its 75 × 23 pixels and read through the numbers.
m06.B2_quote: The values spread across about 9 of the 23 rows all the way through, which fits a large repeating swing within each day.
m06.B3_quote: That's a cycle of very roughly 14 days, close to the spring–neap tide cycle.
m06.B4_quote: At columns 52–55 (around day 43) the values shoot far above the band for about 1–2 days.
m06.B5_quote: Meanwhile the lowest rows go empty for roughly the next 10 days, so the whole level stays raised and slowly settles.
m06.B6_quantity: a water level, most likely tidal (coast or estuary), with one storm-surge or flood event
m06.B8_quote: It enlarges the 1,725 pixels into faint squares and puts the 1,464 dots back. Each column gets exactly as many dots as it had hours, shared among its squares

m07.B1_quote: Matching the image against itself, shifted sideways, showed a strong repeat every 2.496 px. ... I then folded the 798 dots on candidate periods
m07.B2_quote: at 12.42 h they form one clean wave, and at 12.0 h or 24.0 h they are noise.
m07.B3_quote: The spread of the dots grows and shrinks roughly every 14–15 days, which is the spring–neap cycle.
m07.B4_quote: A single event around day 44–45. The whole band rises, with a spike of a few hours about 1.5 times the normal tidal range above the band
m07.B5_quote: A smaller jump and drop around days 53–55, likely also weather-driven.
m07.B6_quantity: sea level from a tide gauge, at a coast with mostly twice-daily tides
m07.B8_quote: The work takes the 798 dots that can still be told apart in the JPEG, finds each one's place in time from its position, and cuts the record into sixty lines

m08.B1_quote: I looked at it, then printed its pixels as text and measured each pixel column.
m08.B2_quote: I scanned the column means for periodic signals. The strongest line is at 12.44 h
m08.B3_quote: the band's width varies in step with the beat between the two, roughly every 15 days. That is the spring–neap cycle.
m08.B4_quote: The spike, around hours 1076–1084 (about day 45), rises fast for about 5 hours, about 30 px above the predicted level
m08.B5_quote: A smaller raised period comes about 9 days later.
m08.B6_quantity: Hourly sea level at a tide gauge on a coast where the twice-daily tide dominates, with one storm surge in it.
m08.B8_quote: I rebuilt an hourly series by sharing each column's observed dark pixels among its roughly five hours ... the form stacks the record as rows of 24 hours

m09.B1_quote: I found the dot centres as local dark peaks with sub-pixel centroids: 1,356 of them.
m09.B2_quote: I searched the series for repeating periods. One period dominates, at **12.42 hours**.
m09.B3_quote: The daily swing grows and shrinks roughly every two weeks, between about 140 and 67 pixels.
m09.B4_quote: Around days 43–45 the daily mean jumps by about 75 pixels for roughly two days, and it peaks on a high tide at about twice the normal maximum.
m09.B5_quote: Around days 53–54 there is a smaller raised level, followed by a sudden drop.
m09.B6_quantity: water level at a coast, from a tide gauge, with weather on top of the tide
m09.B8_quote: 61 rows hold 48 hours each and the colour of every hour shows its level (darker is higher)

m10.B1_quote: I looked at the picture, then printed every pixel as text and measured each pixel column. ... I fitted a tidal model directly to the dark pixels
m10.B2_quote: 12.42 h fitted best by a clear margin (score 0.337, against 0.278 or less for every other period).
m10.B3_quote: Fitting periods to the pixels showed that pattern was a tide, with a 12.42-hour beat and a 14.8-day spring–neap cycle.
m10.B4_quote: one isolated, very high peak at hour 1,082 of 1,464, near a weaker spring tide.
m10.B6_quantity: Water level from a tide gauge, hourly, over two months.
m10.B8_quote: From this I built an estimated hourly series and folded it every 24 h 50 min.

m11.B1_quote: I read every pixel's grey value. The picture is 19 × 6 pixels, so 114 pixels in all.
m11.B2_quote: That suggests a quantity that swings widely and continually, such as with a daily cycle.
m11.B4_quote: Its strongest feature is one fact: a single high excursion around days 42–48 against a broad, steady band.
m11.B6_quantity: I'm not confident about it. ... Temperature or an air-pollutant concentration would fit. ... A river level or flow with one flood is also possible
m11.B8_quote: Each hour's line runs across every band its pixel column shows as inked, at that pixel's darkness.

m12.B1_quote: I found each dot as a local peak of darkness, worked out its centre, and merged duplicates.
m12.B2_quote: I scanned periods from 11 to 14 h and 12.4 h was clearly the best fit
m12.B3_quote: Together they make the range grow and shrink on a cycle of roughly 14–15 days
m12.B4_quote: Around days 43–45 the leftover after the tidal fit climbs over about two days to roughly four times the normal tidal swing.
m12.B5_quote: The level stays raised for a day or two at days 24–25 and 53–54, then drops sharply.
m12.B6_quantity: Sea level from a tide gauge on a coast where the tide comes twice a day.
m12.B8_quote: The 1,464 hourly values are cut into lengths of 24 hours 50 minutes and laid as rows ... with each value shown as a shade
